source.title: Finite-sample analysis of interpolating linear classifiers in the overparameterized regime
source.authors: Niladri S. Chatterji; Philip M. Long

record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes and simulates generalization of an interpolating maximum-margin linear classifier on noisy natural labels, using finite-sample bounds and synthetic experiments rather than the neural-network random-label experiments in V1.
record.gate_note: The paper reports zero training error and test-error outcomes for maximum-margin classifiers trained on noisy Boolean rare-weak data. The plotted numerical values are not recoverable from the supplied text. Comparisons and claims attributed to cited work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study establishes generalization guarantees and simulations for interpolating linear maximum-margin classifiers on synthetic noisy data. It does not compare random-label fitting with natural-label generalization in neural networks (V1), or vary neural-network width (V2). Its own results therefore fit none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate, but sufficient overparameterization alone is insufficient: the guarantees also require adequate class separation and favorable signal scaling. Under those assumptions, maximum-margin linear classification, linked to limiting unregularized logistic-loss gradient descent, can approach the noise-level risk despite fitting corrupted training labels.
record.recipe_differences: Linear maximum-margin classification on synthetic Boolean noisy rare-weak data; no neural networks or random-label experiment. The paper relates maximum-margin training to the limiting direction of gradient descent on logistic loss, and uses exponential-loss gradient descent in its proof.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error varies with dimension, number of relevant attributes, and signal strength γ; with fixed relevant-attribute count it can dip and then rise as dimension increases, while it approaches the noise-level error when s scales as p^0.55 or p^0.65.

fits_no_version.finding: All simulations report zero training error. With fixed informative-attribute count, test error initially decreases and then rises for γ = 0.2 and 0.3; adding informative attributes lowers test error. When informative attributes scale as p^0.55 or p^0.65, test error approaches the noise-level optimum, whereas square-root scaling gives constant test error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear maximum-margin classifiers can interpolate partially corrupted synthetic labels and generalize accurately, with performance depending on signal strength and how informative attributes scale with input dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 4 bounds population error by η + exp(-c||μ||^4/p), with high probability under the distributional, signal-strength, sample-size and dimensional assumptions in Section 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sufficiently separated sub-Gaussian class distributions and suitable overparameterization, interpolating linear maximum-margin classification can approach the label-noise error level.

record.problems: Experiments use synthetic Boolean data and fixed n = 100. The plotted test-error values have no numerical transcription in the supplied text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported for the simulations.

untested.parts: Neural-network capacity to fit fixed random labels, natural-label held-out accuracy under the same recipe, and chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test error when neural-network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The row states indicate that the measures cannot determine any listed version, not that the reported linear-classification effects are absent. No missing results bearing on V1–V8 were identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level test accuracy, the listed neural architectures and datasets, and the same-recipe comparison between random and natural labels.

rows.subject: maximum ℓ2-margin classifier
rows.size_stated: dimension p varied from 100 to 3000; n = 100
rows.operation_detail: Train maximum ℓ2-margin classifier on Boolean noisy rare-weak data; test error plotted against covariate dimension.

conditions.value: first 100 attributes equal clean label with probability 0.7

rows.note: The caption states training error was always 0 and the test-error curve is plotted; the text gives no numerical test-error values.
rows.check: Zero training error on partially corrupted synthetic labels does not establish V1's random-label versus natural-label comparison in neural networks. The supplied text gives no readable test-error values for Figure 1.

rows.subject: maximum margin classifier

rows.operation_detail: Train classifier on Boolean noisy rare-weak data; test error plotted against dimension for each γ.
rows.note: The text says test error has an initial dip and then starts to rise slowly for γ = 0.2; exact values are only plotted. Training error was always 0.
rows.check: This varies input dimension in a linear classifier, not network width or random versus natural labels. The reported initial decrease followed by increasing test error does not measure a listed version.
